deep.reconstruction:
This reading rests on my own numerical checks. Gauss's purpose is not stated on the page and is only partly certain.

LAYOUT. Each row gives a label θ (0, 90, 180, 270, repeated), log10 r, an angle φ in degrees-minutes-seconds, and the complex number x = r(cos φ + i sin φ). There are 15 rows. φ increases from 0° to 180°, so this is the upper half of a closed curve symmetric about the real axis. The labels cycle three and a half times (14 steps of 90°, i.e. 1260° in total).

CONVERSIONS (verified). The conversion log r, φ → x + iy holds in every row I checked:
- 10^0.3478270 = 2.2275477.
- 10^0.5015313 = 3.1734474.
- Row 6: r = 3.25013, φ = 60°20'1.097'' gives 1.60866 + 2.82410i.
- Row 8: r = 2.32496, φ = 79°58'5.059'' gives 0.40500 + 2.28941i.
- Row 11: r = 1.86420, φ = 133°12'52.407'' gives about −1.2765 + 1.3586i.

THE ADDED DOUBLE POINT. 'Dazu der Doppelpunkt' (in addition, the double point) is listed as 0.4013733, 60°0'0'', 1.2599210 + 2.1822472i. This is exactly c = 2^(4/3) e^(iπ/3) = 2^(1/3)(1 + i√3):
- log10 c = (4/3) log10 2 = 0.4013733;
- 2^(1/3) = 1.2599210 and √3·2^(1/3) = 2.1822472;
- c³ = −16.

MY RECONSTRUCTION OF THE CURVE (inferred, not written on the page). Take f(x) = x^7 + 28x^4 − 280. Then f'(x) = 7x³(x³ + 16), so c is a critical point of f. This explains why the curve has a double point there. I evaluated f at the tabulated points:
- Label 0 rows give f ≈ +681.5 (real): x = 2.2275477, and x = 1.7939 + 2.7160i.
- Label 180 rows give f ≈ −681.5 (real): x = 1.5185 + 1.3183i, x = 1.3445 + 2.6824i, and x = −3.1734474.
- The label 90 row x = 2.0496 + 0.5152i gives f ≈ 0.0 + 651.5i.
- The label 270 row x = 1.7688 + 2.4403i gives f ≈ 0.3 − 651.5i (rounding).

So the labels are the 'quadrant angles' of w = f(x). The rows are the points where f(x) is real or purely imaginary along the curve. The curve is the preimage under f of a closed oval in the w-plane, with semi-axes A ≈ 681.53 (real) and B ≈ 651.52 (imaginary).

Why the double point fits. Because f'(c) = 0, the preimage curve has a double point at c exactly when the w-oval passes through f(c). Here f(c) = −192c − 280 = −521.9 − 419.0i, with |f(c)| ≈ 669.3 and arg ≈ 218.8°. That lies between the 180 and 270 labels. It is passed between rows 3–4 and again between rows 7–8, which matches the jump in r (2.01 → 3.01 and 3.00 → 2.32) as the curve loops through c.

The oval appears to be an ellipse:
- (521.9/681.53)² + (419.0/651.52)² ≈ 1.000.
- Its foci are at ±√(A² − B²) ≈ ±200.0. Equivalently, |f(c) − 200| + |f(c) + 200| = 1363.07 = 2A.

In other words, x runs over the preimage of the ellipse |w − 200| + |w + 200| = 2A ≈ 1363.05 under w = x^7 + 28x^4 − 280. Here A is fixed so the curve passes through the critical point. The labels are the eccentric-anomaly angle of w = A cos θ + iB sin θ.

The sheet count also fits. f has degree 7 with real coefficients, so the full preimage covers 7 sheets. Half of it is 3.5 turns of θ, from x = +2.2275 (w = +A) to x = −3.1734 (w = −A).

The purpose ('Zu IV' = belonging to section/figure IV) is presumably a numerically constructed illustration of how the roots of a 7th-degree equation behave along a closed path through a critical value. That may connect to Gauss's later work on locating roots of algebraic equations, but this is conjecture.
errors: No computational errors found. Every row checked is consistent between log r, φ and x + iy to about 1e-6 (row 11 to about 1e-5 given the overwritten digits).
Row 10 omits the 'i' after 1,9931950; this is a notational slip only.
Row 6: 2,824100 is written with 6 decimals; the computed value is 2.8241000, so a trailing 0 was dropped.

results.what: Conversion of polar data (log r, φ) to rectangular complex coordinates for points on a curve
Double point of the curve at c = 2^(4/3) e^(iπ/3) = 2^(1/3)(1+i√3), a root of c^3 = -16, i.e. a zero of f'(x) = 7x^3(x^3+16) for f = x^7+28x^4-280 (reconstruction)
results.modern_name: critical point of a polynomial as a singular (double) point of a preimage / level curve
results.usually_credited_to: classical (Gauss 1799/1849 root-curve arguments; later Riemann-surface monodromy)

results.what: Points where f(x) is real or purely imaginary along the preimage under f of an oval (apparently an ellipse with foci ±200) traversed 3.5 times: tracing roots of a degree-7 equation across sheets (reconstruction)
results.modern_name: root loci / monodromy of an algebraic function along a closed path
results.usually_credited_to: Puiseux (1850), Riemann (1851/1857) for the systematic theory

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a numerical table of points on an algebraic curve with a double point at a polynomial critical point. Gauss's interest in curves defined by polynomial values (fundamental theorem of algebra, 1799/1849) is well known. The reconstruction (x^7+28x^4−280, elliptic path, sheet-by-sheet tracing) is unproven and would at most be a notable computational illustration, not a new theorem.
